65. Cubicle (t), W wall: to the N the access to the triclinium (s) is visible; the circular window, with traces of stucco, opens onto the adjacent alley (Regio II, ins. 4). 78 N47325
64. Cubicle (t), S wall: the fresco has completely vanished, the decorative syntax was repeated as on the N and E walls (cf. figs. 62-63). IV style. 78 N47324
67. Cubicle (u), N wall with access door to the triclinium (s): black plinth with white squares, very few remains of the black middle area.

66. Cubicle (u): black and white mosaic floor consisting of a carpet with a mill blade motif within a checkerboard edge and alternating black and white bands; in the field white tesserae arranged in an oblique warp, leaps in parallel black bands. III style.

68. Cubicle (u), S wall with recessed bed: plinth completely vanished; in the black middle area is visible the candelabrum that separated the decoration between the antechamber and the alcove. III style, phase IA.
69. Cubicle (u), wall O: black plinth with white squares and panels; in the central one opposite triangles, in the lateral squares with rosette; black middle area.

Façade between entrances V 6, 2 and V 6, 1, built in opus incertum and covered with a layer of plaster preparation containing many fragments of amphora, covered with a high protruding plinth of cocciopesto surmounted by an area of unpolished white plaster, inalded under the electoral inscriptions MODESTVM AED SALARIVS ROG (CIL IV 6645), CEIVM SECVNDVM II (CIL IV 6646) and L ALBVCIVM AED CROCVS CVPI (CIL IV 6647).

2. Façade, S corner with the Vicolo delle Nozze d'argento: pillar in opus listatum painted with an intoxicated Dionysus, supported by a Satyr with thyrsus. The god pours drink from the kàntharos to the panther crouching on his right. The electoral inscription under the painting is: CN HELVIVM SABINVM (CIL IV 6649).

1. The counter, with the steps for displaying food, the top covered with marble slabs and the stove for heating food, is also reproduced in plates 8, 10 and 11 of the Antiquités de la Grande Grèce aujourd'huî by G.B. Piranesi (1837). 81 WAS 24511

1. The taberna seen from the S has the façade set back from the other houses of the same insula, and a very large entrance that easily allowed the comings and goings of customers. Large tracts of the completely discolored plaster remain, perhaps red originally. 79 N56523
1. Façade with porch adorned with brick columns covered with stucco, subsequently incorporated into the walls that delimit the shops with entrances at numbers 6 and 8.
2. The façade with the porch adorned with semi-columns and the workshop at number 8, communicating with the atrium (2).

3. Labottega (13) at number 6, to the left of the porch, has a mosaic floor of white tiles with a border of black and white bands and a central square carpet adorned with a floral motif inscribed within a circle, datable to the first century AD.

4. Workshop (13), wall N. The wall decoration, like the floor decoration (see previous fig.) is particularly rich in relation to the function of the room. Above a plinth, the colour of which can no longer be recognised, is a middle area with a central red panel (see fig. below) and panels
5. Workshop (13), wall N. Remains of the apotropaic figuration of Priapus ithyphallic in the center of the wall. IV style.

7. Workshop (13), wall E, section S. Despite the almost complete fall of the overpainted colour, it is still possible to distinguish on the yellow background of the side panel a vignette depicting a cupid in flight playing the syrinx. IV style.
6. Bottega (13), N wall, W section. In the upper area, concluded at the top by a stucco frame with floral motifs, a figure can be glimpsed standing inside an aedicule (Maenad?). IV style.
8. Workshop (13), S. Zoccolo nero wall; middle area moved by the chromatic contrast between the red central panel and the yellow side panels; white upper area. IV style.
9. Workshop(13): in the center of the S wall, almost completely vanished, is a painting representing a Satyr discovering a sleeping Maenad. IV style.
10. The reproduction of the wall illustrated in figure 8 in the Herculaneum Paintings.
11. The painting of the previous figure in the reproduction of the Herculaneum Paintings.

12. Bottega at number 8, floor. Like the workshop located on the other side of the porch and accessible from number 6 (see figs. 3-11), the room, open with a large door to the street, communicated directly with the atrium of the house through the opening visible in the background. As in the symmetrical workshop (13), the decorations are more accurate than is normally found in this type of room. The white floor has a square mat in the center with four-pointed stars placed side by side and arranged in such a way as to form a "coffered ceiling".
13. Bottega at number 8: the threshold of communication with the atrium (2) is adorned with a cord of black tesserae within a lozenge and a rectangle, also outlined in black tesserae.
14. Prothyrum(1), slightly ascented from the road, covered with a pavement formed by 'breaks' of polychrome marble slabs. The flooring is coeval with the wall decorations.

15. Prothyrum (1), wall N: of the pictorial decoration, carried out in the period of the fourth style, at the same time as that of the adjacent workshops, only the last remains of a red middle area are preserved, while in the upper area with a white background there are traces of a decorative scheme with architecture and carpet borders.

16. Atrium (2), view from E. On the W side, next to the entrance to the house, there are doors to communicate with the shops at numbers 6 and 8. On the S wall are remains of the wall decoration. The floor of the vast room is covered with a mosaic carpet of black tesserae arranged in an oblique warp, enlivened by a dense and regular dotted with white tesserae, defined towards the impluvium by a border with a two-strand braid, and towards the walls by two rows of white tesserae. The basin and the edge of the impluvium are covered, like the floor of the porch (1), with fragments of marble slabs. The laying of this floor, as well as that of the porch, must be referred to the last years of the city's life.
17. Atrium (2), view of the E side with the scant remains of the tablinum (11) and the cubicle (4).
18. Atrium (2), view from the S with the door of the room (12).
19. Atrium (2), detail of the floor around the impluvium.

20. Atrium (2): only the S wall retains some traces of the decoration that can be assigned to the phase of the IV style and probably executed, like the floor, in the last years of the city's life, after the earthquake of 62. You can still recognize the high plinth, red in color, and in the middle area a system of large panels separated by compartments: the height of the plinth and the width of the panels are proportional to the size of the room. The decoration of the room is described as follows in PAH I, p. 247: "The frieze" (evidently the plinth) "pretends to be made of marble of various colors; the main part" (the middle area)

21. Tablinum (11), remains of the threshold of passage to the atrium (2), in cocciopesto with diamond ornamentation outlined in white tesserae. The floor of the room, which Pernice describes as being of the same poor quality as that of the atrium, must evidently have been mosaic. 79 N56985
22. Viridarium (14), view from the east with the rooms overlooking it and, in the centre, a masonry basin preserving the remains of the cladding.
24. Room (16), with a cocciopesto floor adorned with a dotted with small white tiles, which Pernice dated to the period of the first style.
23. Viridarium (14), S. Wall Remains of the IV style decoration, with red plinth and middle area with yellow panel with carpet edges.

26. Cubicle (23), floor: the architectural structure of the room, with a raised alcove, typical of the Republican age, is perhaps older than the floor, a mosaic of white tesserae arranged in an oblique warp, with a border in rows of black tesserae in the antechamber and a step of the alcove covered with marble. In the centre of the floor of the antechamber is visible the large gap left by the tear in the figurative motif that adorned it (see fig. 28).

27. Cubicle (23), wall W of the antechamber. The plinth was red, the plinth black. The middle area was bipartite, with panels divided by a central compartment. In the right panel you can still recognize the traces of a painting. Despite the poor state of preservation, the scheme of the decoration allows it to be assigned to the IV style.

28. Cubicle (23): the floor of the antechamber, which came to light in 1784 and was detached three years later (cf. PAH I, 2, pp. 24; 40) bears in the center "a beautiful head of Medusa". AFSN D116486
29. Cubicle (23): detail of the painting visible in figure 27, with traces of a standing figure facing left in profile. 77 N38904

30. Cubicle (23), N wall of the alcove. In the center of the black plinth is a panel adorned with hanging garlands; in the center of the middle area is an aedicule or a large panel with a predella at the base. IV style. 77 N38901

31. Cubicle (23). The W wall of the alcove is occupied, above the black plinth, by a single large panel, in the centre of which are the engravings that delimited a medallion (containing a head ?). IV style.
32. Cubicle (23): on another wall of this room will be placed the painting, with Mars and Venus embracing, accompanied by a dog, reproduced in the Bourbon Museum.  from MB, Vol. I, Tav. 18
33. Cubicle (29). The mosaic floor of white tiles with the use of colored tiles, of which few remains are preserved, was assigned by Pernice to the II style.

34. Cubicle (29). The upper area of the S wall preserves a remnant of the decoration dating back to the oldest phase of the house. The original prominence from the wall of the floor, characteristic of the wall coverings of the first style, was abolished by a subsequent restoration, which involved the area below. The frame also belongs to the first decorative phase of the house.

35. Cubicle (31): detail of the floor, with a central carpet of white tesserae arranged in an oblique warp, border with bands formed by three rows of black and white tesserae, and high marginal flounce, also white.
36. Caldarium (33), with a basin covered with white plaster in front of the W wall.

37. From the caldarium(33), according to the information contained in PAH I, 2, p. 26, the painting with river divinities between two statues of nymph-fountains supporting basins should come, in a scheme that appears very frequently in large garden paintings dating back to the fourth style. The painted decoration, which variously alludes to water (river deity, nymph-fountain), refers to the thermal function of the environment. The painting, donated by Francis I of Bourbon to the French royal collections in 1825, is in the Louvre Museum.
38. Room (35), wall N, section E: on the white background (?) of the middle area, the different traces of colour still allow you to recognise the outlines of a picture (with still life ?).

39. Triclinium (37). Of the floor of this room, only part of the threshold that connected it with the peristyle (39) is preserved, adorned with 'mill blades' outlined in black and white tesserae, a typical motif of the second style. The black and white mosaic threshold 'adorned with two black mosaic dolphins and an anchor in the middle' (PAH I, 2, p. 22, Addenda p. 167), could also date back to the same period. It is also probable, on the basis of eighteenth-century information, which is not easily interpreted (PAH I, 2, pp. 23; 166), that in the center of this floor there were the colored glass tiles now in the National Museum of Naples); (cf. figs. 84-85), comparable with the similar floor of the House of Ephsbo, I 7,11 (see Vol. I, pp. 684-685, figs. 112-113). 77 N38945
40. Triclinium (37), W wall, S section. The remains of the wall decoration, with a yellow plinth and a red middle area, also date back to the second style.
41. Triclinium (37), W wall, section N. Of the II style decoration, with a yellow plinth and a red middle area, the remains of a column can be seen. 77 N38946

42. Peristyle (39): in the center there is a masonry basin, with the walls covered with blue plaster and a masonry podium whose top preserves the remains of a covering with marble slabs. In the foreground is another low masonry basin, with a semicircular niche open in the center of one of the two long sides.  79 N56979

43. Peristyle (39), E. The floor, a mosaic of black tesserae arranged in an oblique warp and dotted with white tesserae, is similar to that of the atrium (2). At the top you can see a column, originally covered with white fluted stucco and later covered with smooth red plaster and incorporated into the pluteus.

44. Peristyle (39): the panel by Giuseppe Chiantarelli (1803) reproduces the complex wall decoration of the W wall - the only one not interrupted by openings - still verifiable on the scarce remains preserved în situ. In the plinth, large panels adorned with wild beasts emerging from plant corollas alternate with narrow compartments, in which kneeling sphinxes support the columns that paratactically mark the middle and upper areas.  On them are painted two-storey aedicules, which in the lower part present, in the center

45. Peristyle (39): the engraving taken from another panel by the same Chiantarelli and reproduced in Ornati 1829, tav. 5, represents the decoration of the N portico, N wall, section O, with the door of the room (48). DAIR 83.1217 28

46. Peristyle (39): portico W, wall W, section S. Remains of the painted decoration, reproduced in the panel of fig. 44, made almost completely illegible by the poor state of preservation of the overpainted motifs. IV style.
47. Peristyle (39): West portico, W wall, S section. Still the remains of the decoration illustrated in fig. 44.

48. Peristyle (39): portico W, wall W, section N. Picture with doors with still life (fish can be seen) that adorned the upper yellow area; the picture must correspond to the one reproduced in the fourth panel from the left of Chiantarelli's panel (see fig. 44). IV style.

49. Peristyle (39): N portico, N wall, W section. Yellow middle area: remains of a small picture with doors with still life, which should correspond to the one reproduced in the second panel from the left in the engraving in fig. 45. IV style.
50. Peristyle (39): N portico, N wall, W section. Stucco cornice with impressed motifs.  IV style.
51. Peristyle (39): N portico, N wall, section E: traces of a floral corolla in the centre of the red plinth. IV style.

52. Peristyle (39): portico E, wall E, section N. The red panels of the plinth were adorned with a kneeling sphinx (left) and a newborn corolla animal (right), but the two motifs are now almost illegible. The middle area was yellow. IV style.

53. Peristyle (39): S portico, S wall, central section. In this image it is possible to recognize on the red plinth the same motifs that appear, almost illegible, in fig. 52. On the left is the wild beast emerging from a floral corolla, on the right the kneeling sphinx. The middle zone is yellow.
54. Peristyle (39): portico E, wall E, section N. Detail of the kneeling sphinx visible in figure 52. IV style.
55. Peristyle (39): portico E, wall S, central section: detail of figure 53. IV style. 77 N38929
56. Peristyle (39): portico E, S wall, section W. Red plinth with panther rising from a corolla. IV style.

57. Room (40), SE corner. Remains of the mosaic floor with a flounce of white tesserae, attributed by Pernice to the late Republican decorative phase (II style), over which passes the partition dividing this room and the room (41); (see fig. 58).

58. Environment (41). The mosaic floor of white tesserae arranged in an oblique warp, bordered by bands of black and white tesserae, which adorned the room (40), later incorporated into the room (41).
59. Room (41), wall E with circular window and remains of a fresco with purple plinth and yellow middle area.

60. Room (43): Serafino Masracchio's panel allows us to reconstruct the appearance of the rich wall covering of the room, in the last decorative phase of the house. The plinth was covered with marble slabs (reconstructed here, but which had already been removed in ancient times, as shown by eighteenth-century excavation reports (cf. PAH I, 2, p. 33); the middle area, of an unusual blue background, had in the center a large aedicule with a painting depicting a "woman's toilet" (H, 1436), in the side panels there were vignettes with figures
61. Room (43), N wall, section E. Remains of a fresco with a blue background; in the upper area a figure can be recognized within an aedicule. IV style.
62. Room (43), wall E. The state of conservation (in 1977) of the wall decoration reproduced in the plate in fig. 60. IV style.

63. Room (43): the S wall retains in situ part of the opus sectile cladding, in front of which some elements of the marble slab flooring are also preserved; in the middle area, remains of decoration with a blue background. IV style.
64. Room (43), S-W corner: detail of the rich decoration of the room, with floor and plinth covered with marble slabs in opus sectile.

65. Triclinium (46), S wall, central section. Despite the poor state of preservation, it is still possible to glimpse the pleasant ornamentation of the black predella, consisting of a hortus conclusus, a garden enclosed by miniaturist reproduced reeds. The motif (which had recently become fashionable, but in larger editions, as in the famous example of the painted garden of the Villa of Livia) continued even in later times, in the phase of the IV style, but in this area of the wall and in these dimensions it is typical of the decorative schemes of the III style. 77 N40422
66. Triclinium (46). Of the mosaic floor, only the marginal bands, with black and white tiles, are preserved.

67. Triclinium (46), S wall, central section. Also in this case the state of conservation allows us to read little more than just the outlines of the images, but the scenography of the large painting placed in the center of the aedicule (supported by slender columns and with an arched roof) refers to some paintings datable, like this one, to the beginning of the first century A.D. and often containing scenes from Greek tragedy.

68. Triclinium (46): the detail of the painting reproduced in the previous figure allows us to distinguish the rich architecture, with porticoes and multi-storey avant-corps, which refer to the royal palaces of tragic scenery, but only nineteenth-century descriptions (Sogliano 554, with bibl.) and the presence of another replica of the same subject, better preserved (National Museum of Naples, inv. 111477,  from house VI 13, 2), allow us to recognize the scene of Medea who convinces Peleus' daughters to chop up and cook their father, promising to rejuvenate him as, thanks to his magic, he did with a ram transformed into a goat.
69. Triclinium (46), O wall, central section: in the black predella, as in the centre of the S wall (see fig. 65), there is a garden with flowerbeds enclosed by reeds. III style.
70. Room (47), view from the S, from the basin in the centre of the peristyle (39), before the roof.

71. Room (47), completely open in the centre of the N side of the large peristyle (39), to which the mosaic floor in the foreground belongs, black with white dots, whose colour tone contrasts with the carpet of white tiles with a border of black and white bands in the room (47). Between the two floors is a white marble threshold.

72. Room (47), wall N. The decoration of the room can be assigned to two different phases, an older one (III style), represented by the niche painted on a blue background, with an oval frame and, in the center of the purple basin, a large stucco shell; and a more recent one (IV style), represented by a plinth with a yellow background, spread over a cavity of tiles.
73. Room (47), N wall, section W. Detail of the yellow plinth, with carpet and dolphin edges. IV style.

74. Room (47), wall E. This wall also contains a niche in the center that was adorned with a stucco shell and completed by marble elements. The black panels with vanid paintings that flank it belong, like the niche, to the decorative phase of the III style. The wall was restored in a slightly later period (phase IV style), with a yellow plinth and a black middle area like the original one, to which it overlaps with a clearly visible detachment.

75. Room (47), wall E, section N. Detail of the yellow plinth restored in the fourth style, containing in the center an aedicule with an illegible motif (bucranium or patera?), and on the left a rampant animal.

76. Room (47), O wall, S section. As on the wall in front (see fig. 74), the niche and the side panels with squares were restored in the last decorative phase of the house by superimposing a yellow plinth and a black middle area.
77. Room (47), O wall, S section: black middle area restored in the IV style. The pink column is covered with floral shoots and flanked by carpet borders.
78. Room (47), W wall. The niche with a blue background with a stucco shell in the basin with a purple background that occupies the central section of the wall. III style.
79. Service rooms of the thermal facility: from the room (34) there was access to the room (50) and the praefurnium (51), from which the heating for the adjacent caldarium (33) came.
80. Mouth of a terracotta cistern in the room (50).
81. Environment (50). Two open ducts in wall E, consisting of overlapping tiles, act as a blowhole of the adjacent praefurnium.
82. Sporadic fragment of mosaic with large white tesserae, resting on a preparation composed of three layers clearly distinguished by their different composition.

83. On the basis of the description of PAH I, ], p. 246, on 15 December, this large fragment of a wall is attributed to this house (room 5A?), detached together with the stucco cornice, now in the National Museum of Naples, (inv. 9701). The fragment represents the central and left part of a rich partition of the IV style: in the center, above a black predella on which a dolphin and a sea monster are painted in yellow, there was an aedicule at the bottom
84a-b. Hexagonal glass tiles, now in the National Museum of Naples, inserted within a modern support, probably from the floor of the triclinium (37) (see fig. 39).
84a-b. Hexagonal glass tiles, now in the National Museum of Naples, inserted within a modern support, probably from the floor of the triclinium (37) (see fig. 39).

The helmet depicted in the centre of the labyrinth refers to the "mosaic floor with a picture in the middle containing a helmet" described in PAH I, 2, p. 29, a notation which, combined with Breton's 1855 report, p. 251, which speaks of a remnant of a labyrinth in black and white mosaic in one of the chambers around the atrium (27),  attribute the mosaic reproduced here to this house (Strocka 1991, p. 106, note 422). da Ornati 1829, Tav. 78

2. Workshop (2): the E wall preserves, up to a third of the height, the remains of a high protruding plinth. Only a small fragment of the first style decoration remains, which was interrupted by the presence of the upper mezzanine floor, supported by quadrangular section beams housed in the appropriate holes, immediately above the window. The door, high and narrow and tapering upwards, is an indication of the antiquity of the construction of the house (IV century BC).

1. Workshop (2): the N wall retains, in the upper left corner, scarce residues of the first style decoration, of which the white stucco top is evident, projecting from the rest of the cladding. The masonry technique of the uncertain work indicates its reconstruction, verified at the foundation level, in conjunction with the construction of the adjoining House of the Vestal Virgins.

3. Workshop (2): the S wall, with a plinth of cocciopesto and plaster, now completely discolored, in which the imprint of the wooden staircase that allowed you to reach the mezzanine remains clearly visible, shows the original elements of the masonry in large square blocks of square work. To the left of the latter are the vertical blocks of the internal doors of the fauces of the Surgeon's House and, in the right jamb, delimiting the entrance, the brick renovations carried out at the time of the expansion of the openings.

1. View of the façade in regular and compact square limestone work, with the high door enlarged (as evidenced by the replacement of the jambs with brick bundles) and preceded by a step added at the time of the raising of the vestibule floor, determined by the installation of the impluvium. Also evident is the seriousness, compared to the square work, of the wall in opus mixed bricks and mirrors of almost reticulated, which delimits the entrance to the workshop at number 9.

2. View of the façade and the perimeter wall S in which the alterations in opus incerta and brick are added to the closure of an arched passage. The grate in front of the entrance covers a stratigraphic test carried out in the '20s, from which the height of the primitive floor levels was deduced.

3. Vestibule (1), detail of the limestone floor in which yellow, purple and green limestone flakes are bedded, according to a technique widespread in the second century BC, the period in which this floor was made, about 0.70 m higher than the previous one.

4. Vestibule (1), N wall, section E located beyond the remains of the sash pier that divided the vestibule from the fauces, covered, like the rest of the wall, with plaster painted with a yellow plinth, the middle area now discolored, in which the imprint of the central architectural foreshortening can still be distinguished, between stretched carpets. The N-E pilaster, towards the atrium, is covered with rudented stucco.

5. Vestibule (1): detail of the central section of the N wall with an architectural foreshortening (the imprint of an aedicule can be seen) and a taut carpet of which the upper and lower arched sides can be recognized.

6. Vestibule (1): the S wall very clearly preserves the signs of the subsequent transformations with the elimination of the door delimiting the vestibule from the fauces, then covered with painted plaster (see fig. 4) in the fourth style and the replacement of the original jamb of the entrance, with a more backward one in bricks, clearly not adhered to the structure in opus quadrata of Sarno limestone. To the SE the pilaster covered with rudented white stucco.
7a. Atrium (5), view from the W that allows you to range from the atrium to the viridarium and to grasp the height of the doors of the rooms (9) and (10).
7b. The same view from the W in an engraving by Francesco Piranesi taken from a drawing by his father Gianbattista.
8. Atrium (5), detail of the tuff impluvium of whose moulded edge, of type A, is very little preserved.

9. Atrium (5), detail of the floor in cocciopesto with white tiles and scattered polychrome flakes, datable, like the other floors of the house, to the period of the second style (beginning of the first century BC).

10. Atrium (5): section between the doors of the rooms (6e) and (6d) with the black plinth now faded, the red middle area in which there was a medallion with a female bust and erotes, now completely disappeared, reproduced in PdE, V, tav. 4.
11. Atrium (5), N wall, W section of the wing (8) with a discoloured plinth and the lower part of a red pilaster marking the end of the wall towards the N-E corner.

12. Atrium (5), S wall, section O with the cubicle door (6b), which preserves the remains of a decoration of the fourth style, similar to that of the vestibule, with a plinth, now discolored, and a red middle area in which the stretched carpets stand out.

13. Atrium (5): the resumption of the S-E section of this room allows us to see the S wall of the tablinum and the E wall of the wing (8a) in opus quadrata. The brick restorations carried out before the laying of the plaster, now illegible, on the wall of the tablinum are evident.

14. Tablinum (7): the view from the viridarium allows you to embrace the entire depth of the house, from the portico (16), in the foreground, to the vestibule (1), passing through the tablinum and the atrium.

15. Tablinum (7): scarce traces remain of the mosaic floor of the second style, with the marginal flounce and the carpet of white tesserae arranged in an oblique warp, and the border consisting of two black bands alternating with two white ones. It belongs to the period of renovation of the floor plans of the vestibule and atrium, coinciding with the installation of the impluvium. 79 N57088

16. Tablinum (7), N wall: plaster painted in the IV style, with the plinth articulated in panels and the middle area with a symmetrical structure with a central red panel with a predella and carpet edges (the vertical sections are staples and circumscribed palmettes

17. Tablinum (7), S wall: at the W end the plaster remains, although discoloured, up to the upper area. Traces of the plinth, now discolored, divided into panels can be glimpsed; of the middle area the large yellow partition is recognizable that closes the lateral architectural foreshortening with a white background at the bottom. The current height of the walls of the tablinum, much lower than the original one, gives a false impression of the relationships between the parts of the decoration.

18. Wing (8): part of the coffered threshold remains of the mosaic floor with square frames juxtaposed by angle and central motif preserved only at the E end, different in the individual panels, judging by the reduced elements of the adjoining one. It is later than the mosaic of the rest of the room, due to the absence of
19. Wing (8), detail of the black and white mosaic threshold: chest of drawers E with a square frame placed side by side by corner and central L-shaped motif.
20. Wing (8), detail of the black and white mosaic floor. In the carpet of white tesserae are arranged, in a zam

21. Wing (8): the N wall has a central panel in the black plinth with triangular carpet edges surmounted by acroterial volutes (?), and side compartments with plants; in the middle area a central red panel, with a purple border, was flanked by architectural views with female figures, closed at the bottom by green partitions (?). In the central painting there was Narcissus (according to what is reported in a manuscript of the Journal of the Excavations from 1763 to 1'784 kept in the Library of the Society of Homeland History in Naples). 79 N56514

22. The sons of Atamante and Nephele, according to the response of the Delphic oracle, falsified by Ino their stepmother, should have been sacrificed to avert the drought that raged over Thessaly; but Zeus, or their own mother depending on the versions of the myth, sent the prodigious ram with the Golden Fleece to save them. The animal, having revealed to them the fate that awaited them, hoisted them on its back and flew towards Colchis, but when they reached the strait that divides Europe from Asia, Elle slipped into the sea, which from then on was called the Hellespont, and in vain her brother tried to save her, extending his hand to her, as Ovid sings (Fasti, III, 871). The painting, on the other hand, shows the young man in an attitude of abandonment, with his arm released, according to a model that recurs in four of the twelve frescoes with the same subject. There is evidently a reference to another version of the myth, in which the fall into the sea is a conjunction in divine marriage with Poseidon, recalled in the figure of the cupid who can be glimpsed behind the girl, as can be the Nereid who appears in the painting of House IX 5,6.
